nameStory: The Rough-legged Hawk gets its name from the feathers that grow down its legs all the way to its toes, giving it a 'rough' or shaggy appearance. This feathery covering helps keep the bird warm during its Arctic breeding season and cold winters. It's like wearing fuzzy leg warmers that extend right down to your feet!
description: The Rough-legged Hawk is a medium-large bird of prey that visits New England during winter after breeding in the Arctic. These sturdy hawks have a chunky build with broad wings and distinctive feathered legs that set them apart from other hawks. They typically measure around 18-24 inches long with a wingspan reaching up to 4.5 feet. Unlike most hawks, they have a unique hovering flight style as they hunt over open fields and marshes.

idTips.label: Feathered legs
idTips.description: Look for fluffy feathers covering the legs all the way down to the toes, giving them a 'boot-wearing' appearance unlike other hawks

idTips.label: Hovering behavior
idTips.description: Watch for their distinctive hovering flight over open areas, hanging motionless in the air like a kestrel before diving for prey

idTips.label: Dark belly band
idTips.description: Many individuals show a prominent dark band across the belly that's easily visible when the bird is perched or in flight

idTips.label: White tail base
idTips.description: In flight, notice the bright white patch at the base of the tail that contrasts sharply with the darker tail tip

idTips.label: Variable plumage
idTips.description: Coloring ranges from light morph (pale with dark markings) to dark morph (chocolate brown overall), but the leg feathers remain constant

idTips.label: Chunky build
idTips.description: Appears stockier and more robust than Red-tailed Hawks, with broader wings and a more compact body shape

habitat: Rough-legged Hawks prefer wide open spaces during their New England winter visits, including agricultural fields, coastal marshes, airports, and large meadows. They're often seen perched on fence posts, telephone poles, or low trees at field edges where they can scan for small mammals. Look for them in areas that resemble their Arctic tundra breeding grounds - expansive, treeless landscapes with good visibility.

seasonality.spring: Most Rough-legged Hawks are heading back north to Arctic breeding grounds by March, though some may linger into early April during late spring weather.
seasonality.summer: Absent from New England during summer months as they breed in the Arctic tundra of northern Canada and Alaska.
seasonality.fall: First arrivals typically appear in late October and November, with young birds often showing up before adults during migration.
seasonality.winter: Peak viewing season when these Arctic visitors are most common, often seen hovering over snow-covered fields hunting for voles and mice.

funFact: Rough-legged Hawks are one of the few raptors that can hover like a helicopter, but they're so energy-efficient at it that they can stay suspended in one spot for over a minute while hunting - something that would exhaust most other hawks in seconds!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with Red-tailed Hawks, but remember the 'fuzzy boots' rule - Rough-legged Hawks have feathered legs while Red-tails have bare, scaly yellow legs. Also watch for the hovering behavior, which Red-tails rarely do.
contextualKnowledge: In Europe, this same species is called the Rough-legged Buzzard, which can confuse American birders since 'buzzard' means vulture in North America. John James Audubon originally called it the 'rough-legged falcon,' adding to the historical name confusion around this Arctic visitor.
compareHints: Unlike the year-round resident Red-tailed and Red-shouldered Hawks, Rough-legged Hawks are strictly winter visitors from the Arctic. They're larger and chunkier than Broad-winged Hawks and lack the rusty shoulder patches of Red-shouldered Hawks. The feathered legs and hovering behavior are unique among New England's buteo hawks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buteo hawks, red-tails are the largest and bulkiest, while red-shouldered hawks are more slender with distinctive reddish shoulder patches and prefer wooded areas.
Among buteo hawks in New England, red-shouldered hawks are the forest specialists with the most distinctive barring pattern.
Compared to its buteo relatives, the broad-winged hawk is the most forest-dependent and migratory.
Compared to our common Red-tailed and Red-shouldered Hawks, Swainson's Hawks have longer, more pointed wings and are built more for long-distance soaring.
Ferruginous hawks absolutely dwarf their buteo relatives – they're significantly larger than red-tailed hawks with much broader wings and a more massive build.
